output.title: Check the exception queue before you automate
output.body:
Before you automate anything, look at the exception queue first. By exception queue, I mean the work that falls out of the main workflow: customer questions that need a different answer, invoice mismatches, data corrections, or similar cases that interrupt the day. If you cannot name that queue, you usually cannot automate it cleanly either.

The useful question is not “can AI help?” It is: which exceptions arrive often enough to justify attention, and which are just random one-offs? For one week, track three things for one queue: how many exceptions appear, how long each one takes to resolve, and what rule the team uses to decide the outcome. Then sort the queue into routine, mixed, or ad-hoc. Routine exceptions are the clearest candidates for a narrow pilot. Mixed queues still need human review built in. Ad-hoc work often stays manual, because there is no steady pattern to lean on.

Keep the control rules visible. If the queue touches approvals, thresholds, audit trails, money movement, or other high-risk decisions, human sign-off stays in place. Automation can organise the review, but it does not replace the decision.

If the data lives in email, spreadsheets, or someone’s head, clean that up before you think about automation. Start by listing one exception queue your team handles manually each week.
